title: Knowledge check: Reading and Setting HTML Attributes

questions.prompt: Which principle best guides a correct implementation of reading and setting html attributes?
options: Skip error handling and assume the default browser state is always correct.
Load multiple library copies and rely on whichever one executes last.

Attributes describe markup; properties represent current DOM state. For example, checked and selected are runtime properties, while data-* attributes are markup strings and jQuery data values are a separate cache.
Render user-controlled strings as HTML so the browser can infer their meaning.
questions.answer_key: Attributes describe markup; properties represent current DOM state. For example, checked and selected are runtime properties, while data-* attributes are markup strings and jQuery data values are a separate cache.
questions.explanation: Attributes describe markup; properties represent current DOM state. For example, checked and selected are runtime properties, while data-* attributes are markup strings and jQuery data values are a separate cache. Apply this principle with the API/version documentation linked in the lesson.

questions.prompt: Which check is most useful after trying the .attr() method?
options: Bind another global handler after every render without cleanup.
Assume the first attempt succeeded and skip verification.
Use a removed jQuery API as the default for new code.
Use the .attr() method deliberately, then inspect the actual DOM, request, or event result.
questions.answer_key: Use the .attr() method deliberately, then inspect the actual DOM, request, or event result.
questions.explanation: A focused observation checks behavior rather than assuming the method call guarantees the intended result. Include an edge case when the state or inputs can vary.

questions.prompt: Which verification approach best supports professional work with reading and setting html attributes?
options: Test a normal path and a relevant edge/failure path, and record expected versus actual behavior.
Test only the first render and publish immediately.
Move answer keys and private configuration into frontend code.
Replace all native browser APIs with jQuery whether needed or not.
questions.answer_key: Test a normal path and a relevant edge/failure path, and record expected versus actual behavior.
questions.explanation: Expected-versus-actual checks, relevant edge cases, and recorded limitations make the implementation easier to debug and review.
